title: The throwaway culture
hook: a culture that discards things and people
carry: nothing and no one thrown away

segments.voice: Yesterday, the cry of the earth and the cry of the poor. Your line was two cries. Which one did you answer, and was the other tangled up in it? Day one thousand three hundred fifteen.

A hillside by the Sea of Galilee. A huge crowd has just eaten, fed from five barley loaves and two fishes. Everyone is full. It would be the natural moment to stand up, brush off the crumbs and go home. But Jesus says to his disciples, in the Douay-Rheims: "Gather up the fragments that remain, lest they be lost." So they walk the hillside picking up leftovers, and the baskets fill. After a miracle of abundance, he cares about the scraps. Pope Francis has a name for the opposite habit, a way of living where whatever is no longer useful gets tossed. Today is that name.
screen: `A CROWD FED ON A HILLSIDE.` → `GATHER UP THE FRAGMENTS.` → `THE OPPOSITE HABIT.`

segments.voice: Francis calls it the throwaway culture. First, it starts with things. Phones replaced while they still work. Food bought and binned. Clothes worn twice. In Laudato Si', Francis points out that nature doesn't work like that. In a forest, what falls becomes food for something else. Our habits, he says, have not learned that cycle, so waste piles up. Second, it doesn't stay with things. This is his sharper point. A culture that gets used to discarding objects slowly gets used to discarding people. Whoever isn't productive, isn't convenient, isn't useful right now. Francis names who tends to be pushed out: the unborn, the elderly, the sick, the poor, migrants. In another letter, The Joy of the Gospel, he says the excluded are no longer even treated as exploited. They're treated as leftovers. Third, the Catholic answer is a different way of seeing. Every person, in this teaching, has a dignity that doesn't depend on what they can do. The baby who can't work, the grandmother who can't remember, the man on the corner with a cardboard sign. Nobody is a leftover. That's why Francis keeps linking the earth and the person: the same eyes that learn to see a broken chair as worth fixing can learn to see a slowed-down neighbor as worth visiting. Fourth, it's practiced in small things. Repair. Mend. Eat the leftovers. Visit the one nobody visits. These look like household tips. Francis treats them as a quiet protest against a whole way of life, and an echo of the care shown on that hillside for a basket of crumbs.
screen: `IT STARTS WITH THINGS.` · `IT SPREADS TO PEOPLE.` · `NOBODY IS A LEFTOVER.` · `PRACTICED IN SMALL REPAIRS.` · then, large: `GATHER UP THE FRAGMENTS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: choose one thing to repair instead of discard. Settle, and breathe. Think of something in your home that's broken or half-used and headed for the trash: a shirt with a loose button, a chair with a wobble, food in the back of the fridge. Decide what fixing it, or using it up, would take. Then let your mind move from things to people. Is there someone in your life who has quietly been set aside? Someone you haven't called because it's easier not to? If you pray, you can bring them to God. If you don't, just hold their name for a moment. The bell holds the time.
The throwaway culture. Francis's name for a way of living that discards things, and then people, once they stop being useful. Today's word.
Your line: nothing and no one thrown away. Today, fix the thing you chose, and send one message to the person you thought of. Day one thousand three hundred fifteen.

howItsDone: Catholics respond to Francis's critique of the throwaway culture in practical ways: parish repair cafés and food-rescue projects, visits to the elderly and the sick, and ministries that accompany people others overlook.
